SAS Studio is free for students through SAS OnDemand for Academics.

title: 1  Introduction to SAS
text:
1.7 What is SAS?
SAS (Statistical Analysis System) is a comprehensive software suite for advanced data analysis, business intelligence, data management, and predictive analytics.
It is widely used in industries like healthcare, finance, government, and education for tasks such as data mining, statistical modeling, and report creation.

1.7.1 What is SAS Studio?
SAS Studio is a development application that runs and processes SAS code on a cloud server. You can access it through any web browser, so there is nothing to install.

proc print data=myclass;

proc means data=myclass;

text:
1.17 General SAS statement rules



All SAS statements (except lines of data) must end with a semicolon.
SAS statements begin with a SAS keyword, such as TITLE, DATA, INPUT, DATALINES, RUN, PROC, and VAR.
SAS statements are not case-sensitive. You can type code in all caps, all lowercase, or a mix of both.
Words in SAS statements are separated by blanks or special characters (such as =, +, or *).

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
2  SAS Tables and Libraries
text:
2.4 The LIBNAME statement
libname libref "path-to-folder";

libref is the short name you will use for the library (up to 8 characters, starting with a letter or underscore).
The path is the folder that holds your data, not a single file.
After this runs, refer to any table in that folder as libref.table-name.

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
text:
2.5 What is a libref?
proc contents data=ma505.overwatch;
run;
libref

A libref is:

a pointer, or shortcut, to existing data
the libref may be deleted, but the data stays in the same place
to get the libref back, run the LIBNAME statement again

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
text:
2.6 Automatic SAS libraries
SAS creates two libraries for you automatically.

  work
    
      default librarytemporarycontents deleted when the session ends
  sashelp
    
      permanent librarysample datasets (like sashelp.class)

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
2  SAS Tables and Libraries
text:
2.8 The Libraries pane
In SAS Studio, open Libraries in the navigation pane, then My Libraries.


WORK: tables you created without a libref, like example. These disappear when you sign out.
SASHELP: sample datasets. Double-click CLASS to view the table you used on Day 1.
MA505: appears after you run your LIBNAME statement. Click Refresh if you don’t see it.

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
text:
2.9 Libraries last for one session

The libref is temporary: SAS forgets it when your session ends. The data is permanent: your tables stay in the folder. Run LIBNAME again (or put it in your autoexec) to reconnect.


So why use libraries?

Short names instead of long paths: ma505.overwatch instead of "/home/u63936157/overwatch.sas7bdat".
Your work gets saved: tables written with a libref (data ma505.clean;) are real files that survive sign-out. Tables with no libref go to work, which is deleted.
One place to change: if the folder moves, edit one LIBNAME line, not every PROC.
Organization: separate librefs for separate projects, or for raw vs. cleaned data.
One line to restore: just the LIBNAME at the top of your program, or nothing at all with an autoexec.

title: 2  SAS Tables and Libraries
section: 2.10 Keeping a library: the autoexec file
text:
2.10 Keeping a library: the autoexec file
The autoexec file is a SAS program that runs automatically every time you start SAS Studio. Put your LIBNAME statement there and the library is ready every time you log in.

In SAS Studio, click More application options (top right) → Edit Autoexec File.
Add your LIBNAME statement (example below).
Click Run and check the log for errors.
Click Save. Sign out and back in to see MA505 waiting in the Libraries pane.


/* autoexec.sas: runs automatically each time SAS Studio starts */
libname ma505 "~";

Reading the output

Skewness (1.25) tells us if the data is lopsided. 0 means symmetric. A positive value means a long tail to the right (a few really high values), and a negative value means a long tail to the left. Anything past ±1 is pretty skewed, so highway MPG is skewed right. Notice the mean (26.84) is a bit higher than the median (26).
Kurtosis (6.05) tells us how heavy the tails are compared to a normal bell curve (normal = 0). A positive value means more extreme values than we’d expect, so a 6 means we probably have some outliers.
Tests for Location (Mu0=0) test whether the center of the data is 0. Student’s t tests the mean (t = mean ÷ std error = 96.7). Sign and Signed Rank test the median and don’t assume the data is normal. All the p-values are below .0001, so we reject that the average MPG is 0, which we already knew! To test something useful, change the value with mu0=: proc univariate data=sashelp.cars mu0=25; tests whether the average is different from 25.

title: 3  Exploring Data with Procedures

3.10 ODS: the Output Delivery System
ODS controls the type and format of the output your SAS code produces: how SAS displays and saves results.

ods trace on; writes the name of every output table to the log.
ods select table-name; keeps only that table in the results.

Exercise: use ods trace and ods select to output only the Extreme Observations table for Damage. Start here, then check the log:

libname ma505 "~";    /* ~ is your home folder; skip if your autoexec does this */

ods trace on;
proc univariate data=ma505.ow_stats;
    var Damage;
run;





/* the log lists "Name: ExtremeObs" for the Extreme Observations table */
ods trace off;

ods select ExtremeObs;
proc univariate data=ma505.ow_stats;
    var Damage;
run;

3.17 Exercise
Use ma505.ow_stats:

For Player 1, in the maps Busan, Nepal, Junkertown, and Oasis, find:

the average number of eliminations and deaths
the top 5 values for damage

Do the same for Player 2.

Hint: a macro variable means you only change one line for Player 2.




libname ma505 "~";    /* ~ is your home folder; skip if your autoexec does this */

%let player = player1;    /* change to player2 and re-run */
%let maps = "Busan", "Nepal", "Junkertown", "Oasis";

proc means data=ma505.ow_stats mean;

ods select ExtremeObs;

4.9 Removing duplicate rows
proc sort data=input-table out=output-table
    nodupkeyRemoves rows with duplicate BY values that sit next to each other, keeping only the first one.
    <dupout=dup-table>;Optional: a table that collects the duplicates that were removed.
    by _all_;Sorts by all columns, so identical rows end up next to each other. You can also list one or more columns.
run;

title: 4  Formats, Sorting, and the DATA Step
text:
4.10 Removing duplicates: example
First, make a copy of sashelp.class with two rows (Jane and Judy) repeated. Just run this; we’ll learn the DATA step later today.

libname ma505 "~";    /* skip if your autoexec does this */

/* setup: sashelp.class plus 2 duplicate rows (21 rows) */
data ma505.class;
    set sashelp.class sashelp.class(where=(Name in ("Jane", "Judy")));
run;

Now remove the duplicates. ma505.clean gets 19 unique rows and ma505.duplicates gets the 2 removed rows.

proc sort data=ma505.class out=ma505.clean
    nodupkey
    dupout=ma505.duplicates;
    by _all_;
run;

proc print data=ma505.duplicates;
run;

4.11 Exercise
Use the Overwatch heroes table ma505.overwatch from Day 2 (re-run the Day 2 import if it’s missing).

Sort it by Player, Date, Win, Map, Role, and Percent Played (descending). Save the result as ma505.ow_hrsrt.

Percent Played has a space, so type it as a name literal: "Percent Played"n

Using the sorted data, remove duplicate rows by Player, Date, Win, Map, and Role only.
What hero is in observation 14 of the de-duplicated data?

Tip: proc print data=... (firstobs=14 obs=14); prints just row 14.






libname ma505 "~";    /* skip if your autoexec does this */

/* 1. sort, highest Percent Played first within each game */
proc sort data=ma505.overwatch out=ma505.ow_hrsrt;
    by Player Date Win Map Role descending "Percent Played"n;
run;

/* 2. keep the first row of each Player/Date/Win/Map/Role */
proc sort data=ma505.ow_hrsrt out=ma505.hero_clean
    nodupkey
    dupout=ma505.hr_dup;
    by Player Date Win Map Role;
run;

/* 3. print only row 14 */
proc print data=ma505.hero_clean (firstobs=14 obs=14);
run;

text:
4.14 How does the DATA step process?

  CompilationChecks for syntax errorsIdentifies the column attributesEstablishes the table metadata
  
  ExecutionReads and writes dataPerforms calculations and manipulations


During execution, the DATA step loops once per row:

Reads a row from the input table (ma505.clean)
Processes each statement, top to bottom
Writes the row to the output table
Loops back to the top to read the next row

4.17 Computing new columns
DATA output-table;
    SET input-table;
    newcol = expression;
RUN;
A new column can be a calculation (Profit) or a constant (Source). FORMAT works inside the DATA step too, and it’s saved with the table.

/* computing new columns in the DATA step */
data cars_new;
    set sashelp.cars;
    where Origin ne "USA";
    Profit = MSRP - Invoice;
    Source = "Non-US Cars";
    format Profit dollar10.;
    keep Make Model Profit Source;
run;

proc print data=cars_new (obs=10);
run;
